pages.cardBlurb: What a bump cap protects against, what it never covers, and the line between EN 812 and a real helmet.
pages.h1: EN 812: what a bump cap actually is.
pages.metaTitle: EN 812 Bump Caps Explained: Protection, Limits & Uses | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: EN 812 bump caps decoded — what they protect against (striking your own head), what they never cover (falling objects), where they're the right call and where only EN 397 will do.
pages.lede: The bump cap is the most misunderstood item in head protection: it looks like a baseball cap, protects like neither a cap nor a helmet, and is exactly right for a set of jobs that helmets serve badly. EN 812 defines what it does — and the limits matter more than the features.

heroMeta.l: You hitting things, not things hitting you
Why vans and racking love it

blocks.html:
EN 812 certifies industrial bump caps: a cap-style shell with impact-absorbing liner, tested to protect against the wearer striking their head on stationary objects — the van roof, the low steel beam, the underside of a conveyor, the racking upright. That's the whole scope. The test energies are a fraction of a safety helmet's, and there is no falling-object protection at all: a dropped spanner defeats a bump cap by design.

Within that scope it beats a helmet on the things that make people abandon helmets: low profile (works in vehicle interiors and voids), lighter weight, breathable comfort for a full shift, and a look closer to uniform than PPE — which is why parcel firms, meter readers and vehicle technicians standardise on it.

faq.q: Are bump caps legal on construction sites?
faq.a: Where the site or task risk assessment requires safety helmets — which is the default on UK construction sites — a bump cap does not comply. Bump caps belong where the assessed risk is striking your own head on fixed objects, not falling materials. The site rules decide, and they almost always say EN 397.

faq.q: What is the difference between EN 812 and EN 397?
faq.a: EN 812 covers bump caps: light protection against the wearer striking stationary objects. EN 397 covers industrial safety helmets: substantially higher impact energies from falling objects, with penetration resistance and optional extras. They are different products for different risks, not grades of the same thing.

faq.q: When should a bump cap be replaced?
faq.a: After any significant impact (the liner absorbs by deforming, and damage isn't always visible), when the shell or liner shows cracks or compression, or at the manufacturer's stated service life. Sweatbands and liners on better models replace separately, which extends the shell's useful life hygienically.

pages.cardBlurb: SNR numbers, muffs vs plugs, helmet-mounted options — and why more attenuation isn't automatically safer.
pages.h1: EN 352: hearing protection by the numbers.
pages.metaTitle: EN 352 Hearing Protection Explained: SNR, Muffs & Plugs | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: EN 352 decoded — what the SNR number means, earmuffs vs plugs vs helmet-mounted (parts 1–3), how to pick attenuation for your noise level, and why over-protection is a real problem.
pages.lede: Noise injury is permanent, invisible and entirely preventable — and the kit that prevents it is labelled with one number almost nobody can explain. Here's what SNR means, how the EN 352 family divides up, and the counterintuitive rule: you can wear too much hearing protection.

heroMeta.l: The at-ear level to aim for

blocks.h2: SNR is a subtraction, not a score
blocks.html:
SNR (Single Number Rating) is the protector's average attenuation in decibels: workplace noise level minus SNR ≈ the level at your ear. A 100 dB workshop with SNR 27 muffs puts roughly 73 dB at the ear — comfortably under the levels UK regulations act on (action values at 80 and 85 dB(A) daily exposure).

The counterintuitive part: aim for 70–80 dB at the ear, not as low as possible. Over-protection isolates — you can't hear the forklift horn, the shouted warning, the change in machine note that says something's wrong — and it drives people to remove protection entirely, which destroys the arithmetic. An SNR 35 plug in an 88 dB environment is the wrong buy; an SNR 20 is right.

blocks.html: UK duties come from the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 — exposure action values at 80 and 85 dB(A). This page decodes the product standard; the regulations and your noise assessment decide what must be worn where. Summary, not legal advice.

faq.q: What does SNR mean on ear defenders?
faq.a: Single Number Rating — the protector's average noise reduction in decibels. Subtract it from the workplace noise level to estimate the level at your ear: 100 dB noise with SNR 27 muffs is roughly 73 dB at the ear. Pick SNR to land between about 70 and 80 dB — protected, but not isolated.

faq.q: Are earplugs or ear defenders better?
faq.a: Neither universally. Muffs (EN 352-1) win for intermittent noise because they go on and off easily and their condition is visible. Plugs (EN 352-2) win for all-day wear, heat, confined spaces and under helmets — if inserted properly, which is a trained skill. Many sites use both: plugs for the shift, muffs for visitors.

faq.q: Can you wear too much hearing protection?
faq.a: Yes — over-protection cuts you off from alarms, vehicle horns and speech, and makes people remove the protection to communicate, defeating it entirely. The target is roughly 70–80 dB at the ear, not the biggest SNR on the shelf.

pages.cardBlurb: EN ISO 11393 classes, Type A vs Type C trousers, and why no garment is chainsaw-proof — it clogs, once.
pages.h1: Chainsaw protection: classes, types and one honest fact.
pages.metaTitle: Chainsaw Protection Standards: EN ISO 11393 Classes & Types | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Chainsaw PPE decoded — EN ISO 11393 protection classes by chain speed, Type A vs Type C trousers, boots and gloves, and why chainsaw clothing stops a saw once rather than resists it.
pages.lede: Chainsaw clothing doesn't armour you — it sacrifices itself. Layers of long fibres pull out and jam the drive sprocket, stopping the chain in a fraction of a second, once, after which the garment is scrap. Everything about the standard follows from that one mechanism.

blocks.h2: It clogs the saw — that's the whole trick
blocks.html: Cut-resistant fabric can't stop a chainsaw; nothing wearable can. Chainsaw protection under EN ISO 11393 (successor to the old EN 381 series) works by clogging: on contact, the outer shell gives way instantly and releases long, tough fibres that wrap the sprocket and stall the chain — typically before it reaches flesh. Two consequences define the buying: the garment is single-sacrifice (any saw contact, however small it looks, retires it), and the protection is rated by the chain speed it can stall, expressed as classes.

items.l: Chainsaw boots carry their own standard (EN ISO 17249) — a saw-rated toe isn't enough

blocks.h2: Washing is part of the certification
blocks.html: The protective fibres only clog a saw if they can pull free — contamination is the enemy. Oil, sap and dried mud glue the layers together; incorrect washing mats them. Follow the garment's label exactly (typically a moderate wash, no softener, no tumble), never patch or sew through the protective zones (stitching pins the fibres), and retire the garment after any saw contact or when the shell is torn through. Our forestry kit guide covers the full head-to-toe system and the sector page the working context.

faq.q: What is the difference between Type A and Type C chainsaw trousers?
faq.a: Coverage. Type A protects the front of the legs (plus small wrap zones) and is the standard for trained ground-based forestry work. Type C protects all round the leg and is specified for arborists, aerial work and situations where the saw can approach from any angle — at a real cost in weight and heat.

faq.q: Can chainsaw trousers be used after being cut?
faq.a: No. The protection works by sacrificing fibres to clog the chain — one contact, even one that looks superficial, means the garment has done its job or lost its integrity, and it must be replaced. Repairs through the protective layers are also prohibited: stitching pins the fibres that need to pull free.

faq.q: What chainsaw protection class do I need?
faq.a: Match the class to the chain speed of the saws you actually run — Class 1 (20 m/s) covers most ground work with standard saws; higher-powered equipment pushes into Class 2 or 3. Employers' risk assessments and training schemes (and any site or utility client rules) set the floor.

pages.cardBlurb: Types, levels and the certification catch: trouser-pocket pads are certified as a pair with the trouser.
pages.h1: EN 14404: knee protection that's actually certified.
pages.metaTitle: EN 14404 Knee Protection Explained: Types & Levels | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: EN 14404 knee protection decoded — Type 1 strapped pads vs Type 2 trouser inserts, performance levels 0–2, the combined-certification catch, and when foam pads quietly stop working.
pages.lede: Knees are consumables in the flooring, plumbing and electrical trades — bursitis and worn cartilage arrive by instalment, one kneel at a time. EN 14404 is the standard that separates real knee protection from packing foam, and it has one catch every trouser buyer should know.

heroMeta.l: Flat floors to kneeling on rubble

blocks.h2: Four types, two that matter on site
blocks.html: EN 14404 covers knee protection in four types; the everyday pair are Type 1 — pads strapped directly to the leg, independent of clothing — and Type 2 — foam inserts that live in the knee pockets of work trousers. Type 1 wins for all-day dedicated kneeling trades (floor layers, tilers): it stays centred on the knee as you move and takes bulkier padding. Type 2 wins for mixed work — always there, nothing to forget, no straps cutting circulation behind the knee — which is why knee-pocket trousers took over the trades.

faq.q: Do work trousers with knee pockets count as knee protection?
faq.a: Only with certified inserts fitted — and strictly, EN 14404 certification applies to the insert and trouser combination, because the pocket's position and fit determine where the pad sits when you kneel. Trousers plus the maker's matching inserts is the defensible buy.

faq.q: What level of knee pad do I need?
faq.a: Level 1 is the working default for trades — tested on flat and uneven surfaces with a penetration requirement. Level 2 adds protection for kneeling on stones and rubble (groundworks, demolition). Level 0 is comfort padding for flat indoor surfaces and shouldn't be doing a trade's daily work.

faq.q: How often should knee pad inserts be replaced?
faq.a: When the foam has visibly compressed, cracked or thinned — for a daily kneeling trade that can be every few months. The insert is a consumable: it protects by absorbing, and absorbed is exactly what old foam no longer does.
